articles.title: Democratic rising star Ossoff projected to hold Georgia seat
articles.summary: Ossoff is seen as a potential leading contender for the Democratic nomination for president in 2028 if he throws his hat in the ring.
articles.preview: Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to have won re-election in Georgia, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and pushing the crucial swing state deeper into Democratic control. Ossoff, a rising star in the Democratic Party, portrayed his opponent as loyal to a "failed president" and made the rising cost of living a central issue in the campaign. Georgia voted for Donald Trump in 2024. Collins had blamed rising cost of living on former President Joe Biden and defended his support for Trump's war in Iran.
articles.body:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to have won re-election in Georgia, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and pushing the crucial swing state deeper into Democratic control.

Ossoff, a rising star in the Democratic Party, portrayed his opponent as loyal to a "failed president" and made the rising cost of living a central issue in the campaign. Georgia voted for Donald Trump in 2024.

Collins had blamed rising cost of living on former President Joe Biden and defended his support for Trump's war in Iran.

With polls suggesting Ossoff held a solid lead in the race, Republicans had diverted resources from Georgia to other contests.

News of Ossoff's projected victory, which was announced less than an hour after polls closed, rippled through the Georgia Democrats watch party in Atlanta with supporters cheering and clapping.

He began his remarks by thanking his family and voters in Georgia for their support, replying "I love you, too", in response to shouts coming from the jubilant crowd.

He returned to many of the points he made on the campaign trail, expressing his concern about the economic woes faced by everyday Americans, while attacking big pharma and corporate America and alleged corruption in the White House.

"This moment is an opening not for restoration, but for reformation," Ossoff said. "And so, amidst our celebration tonight, we must acknowledge that the underlying crisis gripping our Republic remains, and that therefore, our most vital work lies ahead."

The race was one of the first major contests projected as part of the midterms on Tuesday, which will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome will determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.

Brian Kemp, Georgia's term-limited Republican governor, was the favoured candidate to run against Ossoff, but he declined.

Political pundits suspected that Kemp had avoided running, wary of Ossoff's rising star power, with rumours swirling that the Democrat could be mulling a run for president in 2028.

Throughout his campaign, Ossoff downplayed such rumours, saying on multiple occasions that he has "zero interest" in a presidential bid.

His messaging on the campaign trail focused on the economy and voter concerns around affordability, which exit polls show was the top issue for many.

He often hammered Collins, who is currently serving in the US House of Representatives, for voting to support Trump's tariffs which have been linked to rising inflation.

His victory was not unexpected but Republicans had still hoped this would be a more competitive race. It's a state that had previously voted reliably red for decades. President Donald Trump won it in 2024, after Joe Biden eked out a narrow win there in 2020.

An easy win by Ossoff in Georgia could portend a good night for Democrats, though it's still too early to know.

The win could also ramp up speculation about his 2028 plans. The Georgia Democrat is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring.

Daniel Bush contributed to this report.

articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Six hours and 24 minutes. That is how long it took the U.S. Supreme Court’s justices to shut down President Donald Trump’s attempt to intervene in California’s ballot count on the eve of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Usually, the institution takes its time with decisions — mostly over months but even in emergency actions, over weeks — but on Monday, the justices acted with remarkable speed. They gave the administration’s case the same kind of unceremonious treatment sometimes exhibited in matters they apparently deem unworthy of the top U.S. judicial body’s attention.

The court’s decision to deny the administration’s request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who federal officials allege are likely non-U.S. citizens came in a brief, one-sentence order. The court offered no explanation for its decision, and there were no publicly noted dissents among the justices.

articles.body:
Kumamoto – Disaster management minister Goshi Hosono visited on Tuesday areas affected by a major earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture in July.

During his first visit since taking office, Hosono toured an evacuation center that accommodates pets and a bathing facility providing services to people affected by the disaster.

“The central government must support local governments so that differences in their capabilities do not affect areas or people affected by the earthquake,” he told reporters Tuesday, stressing the need to improve conditions at evacuation centers.

Following the visit, Hosono met with Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura at the prefectural government office. Kimura requested that a disaster management bureau, a regional branch of the National Disaster Management Agency, be established in Kumamoto, according to Hosono.

In response, the minister said that he wants to “create a system capable of providing comprehensive coverage across the country.”

articles.preview: Speaking in Antigua, the king did not give explicit support for reparations but said he wanted to ‘address past wrongs’ King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain. “We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday.
articles.body:
King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain.

“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. “We can, however, learn from the past.

“The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth,” he said. “That shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.”

Charles said the more he had furthered his understanding “through listening, learning and looking”, the more committed he had become to building modern partnerships capable of addressing past wrongs.

But the king stopped short of an apology or explicit support for reparations, instead pointing to education, employment, intra-Commonwealth trade and climate resilience as ways of tackling continuing hardship and disadvantage.

“For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us, but we can choose how we set our sail,” he said.

Though speaking as head of the Commonwealth, and this speech would have been drafted by Charles personally along with his advisers, palace aides have indicated there would be “no surprises” in it for the UK government.

Andy Burnham refused to be drawn on whether the UK might offer further financial contributions to the Commonwealth stopping short of direct reparations.

The UK prime minister told reporters: “I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations, and I made that quite abundantly clear in the piece that I wrote in advance of coming here.

“But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got, green finance. That’s what we’ve done under all governments, and in my view, we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth.”

Pressed on whether this could mean additional financial contributions that would weigh on the taxpayer, Burnham said: “Well, you’re getting ahead. What we need to have is that meaningful dialogue where we take time to listen, and let’s be clear: the Commonwealth is an important part of our trade too.

“It’s a two-way arrangement. You know, trade is up between the UK and the rest of the Commonwealth in the last year quite significantly, actually. So you need to see it in that way as well. It benefits Britain to be here, listening to people, building that new partnership, and that’s good for growth in Britain.”

Reparations are not formally on the agenda of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), where trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and opportunities for young people were among the stated priorities of the 56-member bloc.

But sustained campaigning by Caribbean governments and a growing international reparations movement have propelled the issue to the centre of political debate surrounding the gathering.

Opening the summit in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, the country’s prime minister, Gaston Browne, said “fairness” required an “honest engagement with our shared history” and called for meaningful and respectful dialogue on reparatory justice and the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism.

Burnham had said he was open to Britain apologising for slavery, with officials holding talks with national leaders in Antigua about what that could entail.

He has also proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

But Caribbean leaders have stressed that dialogue must extend beyond an apology. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), described an apology as an “essential first step” but said an “apology without repair is incomplete”.

He said any structured dialogue must allow consideration of the entirety of Caricom’s 10-point reparations plan, including public health, education, cultural restitution, psychological rehabilitation, debt cancellation and monetary compensation.

Britain’s royal family benefited from the trade, but Charles is politically neutral and is not expected to offer an apology. A palace spokesperson said it would “not be appropriate” for the king to announce a change in government policy.

According to the AFP news agency, Burnham discussed slavery with the Barbados prime minister, Mia Mottley, during a meeting on Monday, one of several bilateral meetings the prime minister is expected to have at the summit.

They discussed how Britain was “offering a structured dialogue for communities impacted by the transatlantic slave trade”, including the “next steps”, Downing Street said.

Outside the heavily secured summit venue, protesters gathered with placards declaring: “We know what you did and we can see you,” and “You say appalling atrocity, yet you refuse to apologise.”

One protester, Lenworth Johnson, said that if the king’s constitutional position prevented him from apologising, the British government should authorise him to do so. “We feel an apology is necessary,” he said.

Another, Radcliffe Robins, said the wealth enjoyed by Britain and other western powers was built in part on enslavement. “It is absolutely necessary that his majesty the king and the royal family apologise for the brutality and the injustice that they have imposed on us,” he said. “And with that, we ask for reparations.”

Another protester said the demonstration was intended to ensure those entering the summit knew campaigners were “watching them and listening to what they’re saying and what they’re doing”.

Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda Reparations Support Commission and one of the organisers, said: “One whose heart is filled with horror and whose soul bears the most profound personal sorrow must surely be moved beyond words – beyond repeated emotional expression without acceptance of responsibility.

“Genuine moral consciousness demands apologies – the acknowledgment of wrong, the acceptance of responsibility and the commitment to pursue reparations. Unfortunately King Charles III does nothing of the sort. He has again failed the people who recognise him as king.”

The demonstrations followed a reparations event on Monday hosted by the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations alongside campaign organisations.

Its chair, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, welcomed debt relief but warned against presenting it as reparations.

“Reparations was never about personal guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions that still stand,” she said. “Aid is not reparations, because aid leaves the power with the giver. Agency was the crime. Agency has to be the remedy.”

The meeting was followed by a candlelight vigil on an Antiguan beach commemorating enslaved Africans brought to the island. The Rev Bonnie Smith, president of the Antigua Christian Council, asked those gathered to remember people torn from their homes, separated from their families and forced across the Atlantic into enslavement.

“Their names may be absent from our records, but they are not absent from your love,” she said. “Their voices may have been silenced, but their lives have never ceased to matter.”

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, meanwhile framed the campaign as part of a wider struggle for peace and justice.

“We are concerned about the unleashing of terror and violence upon innocent people,” he said.

“We believe that reparatory justice that calls for human decency, equality and justice for all is the philosophy that will hold us together as humanity going into this 21st century.”

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair Campaign, the reparatory justice movement, said he believed Charles’s expressions of sorrow over slavery were sincere, but was disappointed he had not gone any further than his previous remarks.

“The apology hasn’t come. And there’s no talk about reparatory justice. So to that extent, this speech to me was a disappointment,” he said.

The king’s reference to support for health, education and infrastructure, Gonsalves said, concerned subjects already covered in the agreements in the UN sustainable development goals.

“What we are saying is that there has to be, additionally … a special carve-out in respect of reparatory justice,” he added.

articles.body:
Democratic Republic of Congo

The head of the UN peacekeeping mission to Congo, MONUSCO, met with the leaders of the new political and military coalition that was formed last month Tuesday.

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, or FRN, includes rebel groups formerly united under the Congo River Alliance, among them M23, who control large swaths of land in eastern Congo.

It is led by former president Joseph Kabila, who was sentenced to death in absentia for treason and war crimes last year by a Congolese court.

MONUSCO head James Swan met the former president at his residence in Goma.

After the meeting, FRN vice president Bertrand Bisimwa said they discussed the extension of MONUSCO’s mandate, which is up next month.

“28 years later, when you take stock of MONUSCO's activities, you find that it has been a total failure," he said.

"We think that one more mandate would change absolutely nothing for the situation in the country today. We would have liked the mandate to not be renewed and for MONUSCO to continue their retreat as planned.”

M23 is one of about 100 armed groups that have been vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo in a decades-long conflict that has created one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises.

It took control of Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, as well as other key cities in eastern Congo in a lightning assault last year.

Congo, the United States and UN experts accuse Rwanda of backing the M23.

Kabila led Congo from 2001 to 2019.

He took office at the age of 29 after his father and former President Laurent Kabila was assassinated, extending his mandate by delaying elections for two years after his term ended in 2017.

His candidate lost in December 2018 to Kabila’s long-term political rival, Tshisekedi, who has ruled the country since 2019.

Earlier this year, the US government imposed sanctions on Kabila for his alleged role in funding and providing political support to rebel groups operating in the east of his country.

SIHANOUKVILLE: After disembarking more than 200 passengers who had paid tens of thousands of dollars to live on board for years, the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship departed Cambodia early on Wednesday (Nov 4).
articles.body:
Last week, the vessel's owner suspended operations, saying fuel prices increases from the Iran war had made operations prohibitively expensive.

SIHANOUKVILLE: After disembarking more than 200 passengers who had paid tens of thousands of dollars to live on board for years, the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship departed Cambodia early on Wednesday (Nov 4).

Last week, the vessel's owner, Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, suspended operations and forced passengers off the ship at the port town of Sihanoukville, saying fuel price increases from the Iran war had made operations prohibitively expensive.

The ship left with no passengers and around 50 crew, according to Taing Sochitkrishna, head of the Sihanoukville tourism department. He said about 100 passengers remained in Cambodia, while the others largely flew to other destinations in the region.

Passengers unloaded their last belongings from the vessel on Tuesday, and many said they did not expect to return to the ship.

"There are still many things on the ship that I wish I could take with me," said Shirine Thomas, of Wilmington, North Carolina, shortly after collecting some final items.

The Villa Vie Odyssey had been cruising the world for at least 755 days as one of only a handful of ships that offered passengers the opportunity to rent or buy long-term or even permanent residences on board.

The ship's final destination was unconfirmed. Some passengers and maritime tracking websites indicated the ship was bound for Singapore. Villa Vie Residences did not respond to emails or phone calls seeking comment.

Sixty-seven-year-old retired high school teacher Mary Ann Demsar from Ontario, Canada, said the owners had provided no information on whether the voyage would continue.

"We don't get any clear indication from the owners of Villa Vie as to what is happening," she said. "They've been so quiet, the only information we get is from the wonderful government and the representatives here in Cambodia."

articles.body:
Indirect talks continue as Trump says US military struck an Iranian anti-aircraft facility on Tuesday.

Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.

The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.

The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.

Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.

“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.

“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”

His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process“.

He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.

Attack on Qeshm Island

In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.

He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.

“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.

Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.

The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.

The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.

US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.

Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”

In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.

Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.

Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.

Tanker struck in Hormuz

As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.

Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed four tankers had struck mines and caught fire after switching off navigation and identification systems and using what it described as unauthorised routes through Hormuz, and said its forces had seized two other vessels.

That account could not be independently verified or linked to the incident reported by UKMTO.

The IRGC also claimed it had destroyed two US LUCAS attack drones over Bandar Khamir, according to Iranian state broadcaster Pars Today.

John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.

“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.

He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.title: North Korea fires off ‘several’ missiles in latest weapons test
articles.summary: Tokyo did not issue an alert about any North Korean missile launches, as it usually does with those that could pose a threat to Japan.
articles.preview: North Korea fired off “several missiles” on Wednesday, the South Korean military said, as Pyongyang continues to test weapons amid an ongoing row with Seoul. Seoul said its military had “detected several missiles launched from North Korea’s Sondok area toward the East Sea,” referring to the body of water more commonly known as the Sea of Japan. “South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of the exact specifications of the detected North Korean missiles,” it said.
articles.body:
North Korea fired off “several missiles” on Wednesday, the South Korean military said, as Pyongyang continues to test weapons amid an ongoing row with Seoul.

Seoul said its military had “detected several missiles launched from North Korea’s Sondok area toward the East Sea,” referring to the body of water more commonly known as the Sea of Japan.

“South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of the exact specifications of the detected North Korean missiles,” it said.

It was not immediately clear if the weapons fired were ballistic missiles.

The Defense Ministry in Tokyo did not issue an alert about any North Korean missile launches, as it usually does with those that could pose a threat to Japan. This appeared to suggest the tested weapons could have been artillery, a shorter-range ballistic missile or something different.

North-South tensions have soared in recent weeks over a landmine explosion along the two Koreas’ heavily fortified border.

Pyongyang has ramped up weapons tests in recent months, including one of a “dispersal warhead of a strategic cruise missile” that it announced Tuesday. That announcement came just days after it said it had fired off cluster-bomb warheads for its tactical ballistic missiles.

The North fired off around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles on Oct. 29, as part of a demonstration during leader Kim Jong Un’s visit to an exhibition on drone technology.

articles.preview: Growing number of countries are resisting Russia’s reintegration into international hockey after a sports court lifted a ban on competition Canada has joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ⁠ice ​hockey teams from Russia, with prime minister Mark Carney saying Russian skaters will not be able to compete in ⁠a world junior championship next month due to the war in Ukraine.
articles.body:
Canada has joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ice hockey teams from Russia, with prime minister Mark Carney saying Russian skaters will not be able to compete in a world junior championship next month due to the war in Ukraine.

“While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.

Carney’s comments follow announcements by a growing number of national hockey federations that they will not play Russian teams, after a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to allow Russians to compete in International Ice Hockey Federation (IHF) events.

An IIHF ban on Russian teams took effect after Moscow began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has been extended annually.

After several appeals by Russia’s hockey federation, the CAS finally lifted the ban on Friday, contending safety and security worries “were not supported by sufficient evidence”.

On Monday, the Finnish Ice Hockey Association asked other nations to stand up against the decision. Federations representing Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Latvia and the Czech Republic announced Tuesday they sided with Finland.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday thanked European nations for “refusing to share the ice with Russia”.

“If CAS lacks a moral compass, let’s show that hockey still has values,” he said in a post on X. “Refuse to play against Russia and deny visas to its players. Keep Russia off the ice! A war of aggression and hockey are incompatible.”

The Norwegians were the first to announce on Tuesday their intention to play games in tournaments against all teams but those involving Russia.

“Our position that Russia should be excluded from all international championships as long as the war in Ukraine continues … remains unchanged,” Norway’s federation posted to social media.

“At this time, this decision is based on our responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of our players, team staff and their families. We believe playing against Russia under the current circumstances could expose our players and team staff to significant security risks.”

Similar statements followed from the other three nations.

The CAS ruling has left cities worldwide to decide whether they will host upcoming tournaments, as planned, should Russians compete as the war continues in Ukraine.

The world junior tournament is scheduled to begin 26 December in Alberta.

articles.title: Russia bombards Ukraine power grid before Abu Dhabi talks; Merz urges Moscow to engage
articles.summary: In more than four years of war, Russia has repeatedly targeted the Ukrainian energy system as winter approaches.
articles.preview: KYIV/BERLIN – Russia bombarded Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in waves on Tuesday, knocking out power to swathes of the country with dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones, a week before U.S.-brokered peace talks were due to resume. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at least 33 people had been killed on Monday when Russia twice bombed a school being used for aid distribution in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region. About 50 people were still believed to be buried under the rubble, he said.

KYIV/BERLIN – Russia bombarded Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in waves on Tuesday, knocking out power to swathes of the country with dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones, a week before U.S.-brokered peace talks were due to resume.

articles.title: Palazzo Chigi: "In Italia impatto limitato dell'attacco hacker solo ai sistemi obsoleti"
articles.summary: AGI - L’ attacco hacker che ha interessato migliaia di attività commerciali mandando in tilt i sistemi di refrigerazione in Europa ha interessato in maniera estremamente limitata l’ Italia . È quanto emerge dalla riunione che si è svolta a Palazzo Chigi con il sottosegretario alla presidenza del Consiglio, Alfredo Mantovano , e il ministro dell' Agricoltura , Francesco Lollobrigida , alla quale hanno partecipato il direttore dell' Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale (ACN) e i direttori delle Agenzie di intelligence . Dai primi accertamenti, si legge in una nota di Palazzo Chigi , "emerge che in Italia l'impatto degli attacchi è al momento fortemente limitato: sono state interessate poche unità commerciali, a fronte delle migliaia presenti sull'intero territorio nazionale, per lo più munite ancora adesso di sistemi di sicurezza obsoleti , con interfacce esposte direttamente su Internet e carenze nei meccanismi di autenticazione". Abbiamo sistemi di protezione aggiornati "La gran parte della catena di distribuzione - sottolinea la presidenza del Consiglio - risulta invece dotata di sistemi di protezione aggiornati , in grado di respingere intrusioni malevole. Non è emerso alcun caso di rischio per la salute dei cittadini riconducibile a fenomeni di scongelamento. Ogni eventuale segnalazione di anomalia viene peraltro notificata dall' ACN ai NAS dei carabinieri , al fine di garantire tempestivi interventi. L' ACN - si legge ancora - sta inoltre incontrando i rappresentanti delle categorie interessate e gli amministratori dei principali operatori del settore. Il Governo , in tutte le sue articolazioni, continuerà ad agire lungo quattro direttrici: monitoraggio e analisi della minaccia, attività peraltro avviata già da mesi; interlocuzione costante con i fornitori e i venditori della filiera alimentare ; individuazione e tempestiva notifica dei soggetti esposti; diffusione su larga scala di comunicazioni preventive e indicazioni per la mitigazione dei rischi nei settori interessati". "Non sussiste quindi alcun allarme, ma permane la massima attenzione da parte di tutti i soggetti istituzionali competenti", conclude la nota. Acn, "rafforzata la collaborazione con la filiera della distribuzione" L'incontro di oggi con gli operatori della filiera della distribuzione alimentare ha avuto l'obiettivo di "favorire il coordinamento e rafforzare la collaborazione tra i soggetti coinvolti nella gestione delle minacce informatiche che interessano il settore". L' Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale spiega che al vertice hanno preso parte rappresentanti del ministero dell'Agricoltura, della Sovranità alimentare e delle Foreste e alcuni tra i principali gruppi e operatori della distribuzione e dell'industria alimentare, tra cui Assocold, Agricola Italiana alimentare, Coop, Conad, Federdistribuzione, Barilla, Gros, Galbani, Esselunga, GS, Marr,MD, Metro, Pam Pamorama, Unicoop Firenze. Nel corso della riunione - spiega l'Acn - i partecipanti hanno espresso "apprezzamento per l'iniziativa dell'Agenzia e per l'opportunità di un confronto comune", riconoscendo "il valore della collaborazione tra operatori e della condivisione tempestiva delle informazioni quale elemento essenziale per rafforzare la capacità di prevenzione e risposta agli attacchi informatici". L'incontro è stato utile anche per ipotizzare la costituzione di un Isac (Information sharing and analysis center) di settore, che integrato con l'Isac Italia istituito presso l'Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale, rappresenterebbe "un punto unico di condivisione rapida di informazioni relative alla minaccia cyber indirizzata allo specifico comparto e consentirebbe di innalzare ulteriormente la capacita' di risposta e resilienza per un altro settore critico per il Paese".

articles.title: Centrosinistra al lavoro sul programma, restano i nodi Ucraina e patrimoniale
articles.summary: AGI - Palla ai capigruppo sul tavolo del centrosinistra. I leader di Pd, M5s e Avs hanno deciso di affidare ai luogotenenti alle Camere il calcio d'inizio della partita sul programma. Saranno Chiara Braga e Francesco Boccia per il Pd, Riccardo Ricciardi e Luca Pirondini per M5s, Luana Zanella e Peppe De Cristoforo per Avs, Maria Elena Boschi e Raffaella Paita per Italia Viva, a istruire il lavoro sulle proposte che i progressisti presenteranno agli elettori. A questi si aggiungono i rappresentanti delle forze che non hanno gruppi costituiti in Parlamento: Riccardo Magi per Più Europa, Ernesto Ruffini e Franco Gabrielli per Più Uno, e il responsabile del programma di Progetto Civico, Marco Mistretta . Le basi dell'intesa tra le opposizioni Una scelta, quella dei leader, che nasce da un dato di fatto: è proprio dentro e tra i gruppi parlamentari che sono nate le proposte unitarie sulle quali si è costruita in questi anni l'unità del centrosinistra, dalla mozione dell'aprile 2025 sulla Palestina alla risoluzione sul Dpfp, con i ventuno punti economici e sociali, presentata lo scorso mese. Il tavolo, poi, sarà allargato ad altri esponenti, anche in base ai temi trattati. Infine, scenderanno in campo i leader, entro la fine di novembre, stando a quanto emerso venerdì durante la call fra Giuseppe Conte , Elly Schlein , Nicola Fratoianni e Angelo Bonelli . L'assemblea del 5 novembre Nell'attesa di vedersi al tavolo, i leader si ritroveranno sullo stesso palco giovedì 5 novembre in occasione dell'Assemblea di programma - Il Futuro è adesso . Oltre a Elly Schlein , Giuseppe Conte , Angelo Bonelli e Nicola Fratoianni ci saranno Maria Elena Boschi , Riccardo Magi e il segretario della Cgil, Maurizio Landini . Conte: "Abbiamo atteso anche troppo" Un percorso per il programma che il leader M5s vorrebbe il più veloce possibile, come è tornato a sottolineare anche oggi, rispondendo a chi lo ha incontrato alla Camera. "Abbiamo atteso anche troppo", ha detto Conte attribuendo implicitamente la responsabilità del ritardo agli alleati dem: "L'intoppo? Siete voi che seguite il Pd", ha risposto ai giornalisti. Ora, ha aggiunto, la priorità è quella di dare "segnali forti" per "rispondere ai bisogni dei cittadini" . Il nodo Ucraina e il confronto sulle tasse Il nodo rimane quello dell'Ucraina e dell'invio di armi a Kiev, che vede contrari M5s e Avs, con il Pd che chiede di accompagnare gli aiuti con un vero sforzo diplomatico europeo. Non preoccupano, invece, a sondare fonti dei partiti, i diversi punti di vista emersi nelle ultime ore, "più sulle pagine dei giornali che nel confronto fra i partiti", per dirla con una dirigente dem, riguardanti la patrimoniale, cavallo di battaglia di Nicola Fratoianni , e la legalizzazione della cannabis che il segretario di Più Europa, Riccardo Magi , assicura di voler portare al tavolo del programma. "Di queste cose parliamo ai tavoli che adesso sono partiti, ci sono i nostri rappresentanti, già in settimana si riuniranno e inizieranno a lavorare concretamente", taglia corto Conte che sulla patrimoniale aggiunge: "Noi abbiamo delle proposte per quanto riguarda una seria redistribuzione". Lo strumento della patrimoniale non convince nemmeno i dem: Elly Schlein ha sottolineato, fin dalla sua mozione congressuale, che non si tratta di "un tabù", ma a certe condizioni. La prima è che sia adottata a livello europeo o internazionale, come sottolineato durante una tavola rotonda su fisco e diseguaglianze alla Treccani, nel febbraio 2025. La battaglia parlamentare sulla Palestina Uno dei "segnali forti" chiesti da Conte, intanto, arriva dall'Aula della Camera dove le opposizioni chiedono unitariamente al governo e alla maggioranza di mettere la faccia su quanto accade in Cisgiordania. La proposta è quella di dare carattere di urgenza alla proposta di legge per il blocco immediato degli scambi di beni e servizi con le colonie israeliane in Cisgiordania. A illustrare la richiesta è Nicola Fratoianni di Avs: "Chiediamo l'urgenza su questa legge perché vogliamo che l'Italia faccia la sua parte, la parte giusta nella storia e nel mondo che viviamo. L'8 settembre 2026 una coalizione di 12 Paesi, tra i quali Canada, Regno Unito, Spagna, Irlanda, Norvegia e Danimarca, ha annunciato misure di restrizione commerciale sui prodotti provenienti da colonie nella Cisgiordania occupata. Contro quello che il governo fascista di Netanyahu mette in campo contro i palestinesi". Il tavolo, poi, sarà allargato ad altri esponenti, anche in base ai temi trattati. articles.body:
Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.

In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, the US president said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it”.

“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.

Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”

During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”

Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.

Israeli officials appeared to be taken by surprise by the announcement, and leading members of the opposition said it showed the damage that Netanyahu had done to the US-Israel relationship. The announcement comes at a crucial moment after Netanyahu’s party lost its majority in the Knesset in last week’s elections and the opposition is trying to cobble together a coalition to replace him.

“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” said Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right rival to Netanyahu who is seeking to replace him as prime minister. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”

“A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase American aid, not dismantle it,” wrote Yair Golan, the head of the Democrats opposition party. “Netanyahu is deepening the security and economic crisis, putting Israel’s future at risk.”

Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as foreign military financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.

Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, in which US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.

Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”

During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

articles.title: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.summary: At least 38 people are killed in 24 hours and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky warns dozens more could be trapped under rubble.
articles.preview: Russian strikes on Ukraine â including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital â have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours. At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble. He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Ukraine â including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital â have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.

At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.

He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".

Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.

The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.

Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.

Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof collapsed, trapping many underneath.

"The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.

Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen.

However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.

The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment.

According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital.

But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law", external.

Further north, in Dnipro, nearly 50 terminally ill patients were being transferred to other facilities after their hospice was destroyed by a Russian missile on Monday night. The oldest of the patients was 90 years old.

Mayor Boris Filatov posted photos on Telegram showing elderly people lying in their beds in a hospice room with blown-out windows and rubble and broken glass strewn on the floors.

"I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad.

"These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."

Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.

Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating.

The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".

As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.

It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.

Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.

Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.

US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting., external

The UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities.

At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.

In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

articles.title: Russian bombing kills 31 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
articles.summary: Officials say at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a southern Ukrainian village in what the president calls an "utterly horrific" attack.
articles.preview: At least 31 people have been killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre in Zaporizhia, the Ukrainian regional head has said, describing it as one of the deadliest attacks there since the start of the full-scale invasion. Mykhailo Semikin said at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in southern Ukraine on Monday and the aid centre collapsed from a "direct hit".
articles.body:
At least 31 people have been killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre in Zaporizhia, the Ukrainian regional head has said, describing it as one of the deadliest attacks there since the start of the full-scale invasion.

Mykhailo Semikin said at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in southern Ukraine on Monday and the aid centre collapsed from a "direct hit".

"They had come for help - not to a military facility, not to a frontline position, but to a place where they were supposed to receive support," he wrote on Telegram.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the attack "utterly horrific" and said there were still people "under the rubble".

Zelensky posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack and rescuers searching for survivors.

However, officials say teams have at times been forced to halt their search because of Russian drone attacks in the area.

Zelensky said after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.

He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.

The Russian military has not publicly commented.

Three days of mourning have been declared in the region.

The death toll has continued to rise on Tuesday. Earlier, when 29 people were confirmed to have died, Semikin said another 10 had been injured and 48 were reported missing.

Among the dead are two rescuers and four police officers, according to Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS.

Zelensky said the attack was "yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation".

He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".

"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, next week, US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff said on X.

Since the talks were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

No major breakthrough is expected at the talks. Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace".

Witkoff said US negotiators would also meet European and Nato officials this week in Brussels.

articles.title: Can US midterm election really change Trump's Iran policy?
articles.summary: The US midterms are at hand, but their impact on the Iran war remains far from clear. Analysts say the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears.

articles.body:
November 3, 2026

The US midterms are at hand, but their impact on the Iran war remains far from clear. Analysts say the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears.

Tuesday's election is shaping up to be one of the most consequential midterm votes in modern US history, with Washington's relationship with Israel and its war on Iran at the center of the political standoff.

Many Democrats, including the party's rising stars such as Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, are outspoken critics of the Iran war. El-Sayed called the conflict "illegal" and "stupid."

US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the effects of the war during the campaign. Last week, he claimed only "one or two targets" remained in Iran and that those could be settled in 10 minutes. However, he immediately added that messages were still being exchanged, Tehran still shows strong interest in a deal, and the US has plenty of time to deal with the crisis.

At the same time, there are reports of the US and Israel preparing to launch a new round of strikes on Iran just after the midterm election . Pro-war Republicans such as Senator Ted Cruz are putting pressure on the White House to deal with "the threat" posed by Iran.

"I have urged arming the Iranian protesters to overthrow the regime," Cruz said in an online post after spending a day with Trump.

Behind the scenes, analysts warn that the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears. Moreover, even a resounding Democrat victory might not give them enough leverage on the Trump administration regarding the Iran war.

Democrats and Republicans broadly 'in consensus' on Iran

Talking to DW, former National Security Advisor John Bolton said the Democrats are likely to secure a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, handing them control of the Iran war funding.

The US Congress "can allocate defense budgets or impose restrictions on the use of financial resources," Bolton said.

Nevertheless, Bolton pointed out that the US president can veto congressional legislation, which would then require a two-thirds majority in both assemblies to overcome.

"Even if Democrats hold a majority in both houses, their influence will be limited to the legislative and political tools of Congress," he said.

US diplomat and Iran expert Alan Eyre, a fellow at the Middle East Institute, described a kind of "bipartisan consensus" that Republicans and Democrats have on Iran.

"Both major US parties share significant common ground in their opposition to the political structure of the Islamic Republic and in their support for policies aimed at exerting pressure on Tehran to change its behavior," he said.

What does Tehran think?

While warning of a "crushing response" to any new strikes on underground sites, Tehran has confirmed ongoing indirect communication via Doha and Muscat, keeping its diplomatic option open.

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst leading the Iran team at ITSS Verona, told DW that Tehran's actions are based on a miscalculation. The regime, he argued, assumes that a Democratic Congress can easily restrain the White House.

Tehran's strategy in dragging out peace talks, pressuring the Strait of Hormuz, and letting fuel prices weigh on US voters, aims to deny Trump a win before November. However, Modarres noted this strategy may backfire after the election, when the Trump administration will no longer have any reason to delay its moves.

This approach also ignores the fact that both US parties largely agree on not letting Iranian develop nuclear weapons, he said.

Will Trump launch new strikes and declare victory?

Trump's ally-turned-critic John Bolton believes the president will only decide on his next steps on Iran after the election, once the political pressure grows less acute.

"I cannot predict what the US President will do; even Trump himself does not know his final decision right now," he told DW.

Bolton cites as an example a possible US attack on "Kuh-e Kolang," the new nuclear site he claims the Iranian government is constructing near Natanz.

"In this scenario, Trump could damage these facilities, declare victory, and pull back."

Bolton: 'Regime change' only guarantee against Iran getting nukes

Trump has consistently emphasized that the US goal is to deny Iran the capability of acquiring nuclear weapons. Throughout the conflict, the US president has also repeatedly claimed his administration had succeeded in this regard.

Bolton, in contrast, believes that the Islamic Republic will continue to pursue nuclear weapons capability for as long as it remains in power.

The former Trump advisor views "regime change" as the only sustainable solution to keep Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

US failing to communicate with ordinary Iranians

Eyre emphasized the difficulty of using external tools to bring about sustainable change. In his view, even if there is a consensus in Washington opposing the Islamic Republic and demanding a change in its behavior, this US consensus alone cannot overcome the structural obstacles to political change inside Iran. He reiterated that any fundamental transformation must emerge from within Iranian society itself.

The veteran diplomat also pointed to the failure of American diplomacy to "convey a clear, coherent, and authentic message to Iranian society."

He noted that official US government messaging is only incompletely reflected in the media outlets that the vast majority of Iranian citizens rely on for news.

"Furthermore, targeted and principled engagement with the core of Iranian society has generally not been a priority for successive US administrations," he said. "Iranian citizens see that the US takes certain positions at the rhetorical level, but behaves differently in practice."

According to Eyre, this gap between words and deeds in Washington is a structural phenomenon that is not limited to a single administration or a single election cycle.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

articles.title: Perché Gaza non ha contato nel voto degli israeliani
articles.summary: Le due principali coalizioni che si sono sfidate alle elezioni del 27 ottobre la pensano allo stesso modo sulla guerra e l’occupazione dei territori palestinesi
articles.preview: Il parlamento israeliano rimane in una situazione di stallo. Con il voto del 27 ottobre, che ha registrato l’affluenza alle urne più alta degli ultimi decenni, né la coalizione del primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu né quella che si è chiamata alleanza di opposizione sionista hanno conquistato i 61 seggi necessari per avere la maggioranza in parlamento. Il campo di Netanyahu è arrivato primo, con 53 seggi, cinque in più del principale blocco di opposizione.
articles.body:
Il parlamento israeliano rimane in una situazione di stallo.

Con il voto del 27 ottobre, che ha registrato l’affluenza alle urne più alta degli ultimi decenni, né la coalizione del primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu né quella che si è chiamata alleanza di opposizione sionista hanno conquistato i 61 seggi necessari per avere la maggioranza in parlamento.

Il campo di Netanyahu è arrivato primo, con 53 seggi, cinque in più del principale blocco di opposizione. I partiti arabi sono saliti a 19 seggi, un risultato storico, ma sono stati relegati a meri osservatori delle trattative per la coalizione di governo.

Visti da fuori, questi risultati potrebbero apparire sorprendenti.

Le riforme giudiziarie introdotte all’inizio del mandato di Netanyahu nel 2022 avevano provocato le più imponenti proteste di piazza della storia israeliana, e ancora oggi il primo ministro è coinvolto in un processo per corruzione risalente al 2019.

Nessuno è stato chiamato a rendere conto dei presunti fallimenti in relazione agli attacchi di Hamas del 7 ottobre 2023, che hanno scatenato la guerra di Israele contro i palestinesi della Striscia di Gaza, nonostante le forti pressioni popolari.

Inoltre, il genocidio ha generato un crescente isolamento internazionale, fornendo anche il pretesto per molti attacchi a diversi paesi in tutta la regione, l’ultimo dei quali, lanciato contro l’Iran a febbraio insieme agli Stati Uniti, continua a scuotere i mercati energetici mondiali.

Eppure, circa 2,38 milioni di israeliani sono andati alle urne per sostenere la coalizione di Netanyahu guidata dal suo partito, il Likud, mentre 2,21 milioni hanno votato per l’alleanza di opposizione.

Entrambe le coalizioni hanno dedicato poco spazio a parlare dei molti crimini di guerra di cui è accusato Israele a Gaza, dove gli attacchi israeliani hanno ucciso più di 74.500 persone e gran parte del territorio è in macerie. Né hanno preso in considerazione la complicità del governo nell’aumento di violenze e pogrom nella Cisgiordania occupata, dove una commissione d’inchiesta delle Nazioni Unite ha dichiarato il 26 ottobre che Israele sta compiendo crimini contro l’umanità, tra cui sterminio, tortura e stupro.

Secondo gli analisti, il fatto che né Gaza né la Cisgiordania siano stati un fattore decisivo nelle scelte elettorali degli israeliani è dipeso in gran parte dal fatto che su questi temi esiste un vasto consenso tra le due coalizioni.

La campagna elettorale invece si è combattuta su questioni in gran parte interne: il potere dei tribunali israeliani, l’esenzione degli ultra-ortodossi dal servizio militare e l’eventualità di un’inchiesta sulle presunte responsabilità del governo israeliano nell’aver trascurato i segnali che preannunciavano l’attacco del 7 ottobre 2023.

Meccanismo di negazione

Il noto sociologo israeliano Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani spiega che le questioni sono state presentate all’opinione pubblica israeliana con un’impostazione sostanzialmente simile a quella dei politici al governo.

“Non credo che il problema sia semplicemente la disinformazione o il disimpegno delle persone”, afferma. “Molti israeliani sanno che Gaza è stata devastata, anche se sono esposti a una rappresentazione molto selettiva di quella devastazione. Ma una cosa è conoscere una realtà, un’altra è comprenderne le implicazioni morali e politiche”, aggiunge, spiegando così l’assenza di empatia mostrata da molti israeliani di fronte alla ben documentata sofferenza dei palestinesi a Gaza.

“Cittadini comuni, che amano le loro famiglie, si preoccupano per i loro amici e si considerano persone perbene, possono anche prendere parte o avallare un ordine politico che produce sofferenze immani per altri”, commenta.

Secondo Shenhav-Shahrabani è stato messo in atto “un potente meccanismo di negazione”: “Non necessariamente una negazione dei fatti, ma una negazione del loro significato”.

Per i sostenitori di Netanyahu, tuttavia, questo rifiuto potrebbe essere ricondotto a qualcosa di più personale.

“Il Likud è una tribù, forse anche una setta, e per chi ne fa parte il leader ha sempre ragione”, dice l’analista israeliano Ahron Bregman a proposito della base del primo ministro, che l’ha sostenuto per un totale di diciannove anni, quasi un quarto di tutta la storia di Israele. “Per loro il nemico, subito dopo gli arabi, è la sinistra, e voterebbero per Netanyahu nonostante tutti i suoi difetti”, aggiunge Bregman, che insegna al King’s college di Londra.

Per la gran parte di questo elettorato, il voto non è stato tanto un giudizio sull’operato del governo quanto una scelta tra rivendicazioni contrastanti di legittimità politica, o come dice lo studioso Roi Zur, una lotta per “l’essenza della democrazia” e il futuro dell’identità ebraica e israeliana.

“La cosa più importante, credo, per l’affluenza tra i sostenitori di Netanyahu è l’idea che la coalizione alternativa sarebbe più debole sul tema della sicurezza”, spiega Zur, esperto di comportamenti elettorali che insegna all’università dell’Essex.

Secondo lui, Netanyahu è riuscito particolarmente bene a creare “una campagna di paura e la convinzione che solo lui è in grado di gestire questa situazione, che lui è l’unico primo ministro abbastanza forte. L’idea è che Netanyahu sia l’unico leader, il più forte, in grado di guidare Israele in questa fase e in particolare nel periodo successivo alla guerra del 7 ottobre”.

Guerra e occupazione, secondo Shenhav-Shahrabani, non erano scelte da considerare andando alle urne. Piuttosto, sono diventate il prisma attraverso il quale nei decenni gli israeliani hanno imparato a interpretare “la sicurezza, la cittadinanza e il significato stesso della democrazia”. Per questo, conclude, “sostituire Netanyahu, per quanto importante, non risolverà di per sé il problema di fondo”. ◆

articles.title: Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?
articles.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.
articles.preview: November 3, 2026 France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments. With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.
articles.body:
November 3, 2026

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

Battle for investor capital heats up

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

European companies could also feel more pain

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

Regional governments paying the price for AI

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

articles.title: 'Fuel of the poor' LPG soars in Pakistan, forcing rickshaw drivers to cut meals

Traders said the price of a 12kg cylinder surged 56 per cent to 7,000 Pakistani rupees (US$25.30) within days of border closures triggered by the war in Iran, or about 583 rupees per kg on the open market.

LAHORE: For 13 years, Rashid Ali has driven a three-wheeled motorised rickshaw around Lahore in eastern Pakistan.

His day starts at 6am and sometimes does not end until midnight, but he was long able to make US$6.50 a day - enough for his family's bare essentials. Now, with liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices surging he doesn't even make half that.

Ali, 33, is among thousands of Pakistani drivers who run their vehicles on LPG, which is sold in cylinders and mainly used for cooking and heating.

Majeed Ghauri, chairman of the Awami Rickshaw Union, calls it "the fuel of the poor." He said about 70 per cent of its members' 43,000 auto-rickshaws and nearly 8,000 Qingqis - motorcycle-based three-wheelers that carry several passengers on set routes - run on LPG.

LPG prices have surged since Oct 17, when two Iranian border crossings closed, halting imports, traders say, in the latest energy shock since the US-Iran war began in February.

With Ali now lucky to make US$3 a day, his family has cut back on meals, eating only twice a day.

"Previously, when LPG was cheap, we could earn a decent income," Ali said. "Now, it's just not possible to get by on seven or eight hundred (rupees), is it?"

Before the border closures, Pakistan imported about 7,000 metric tons of LPG a day from Iran, the Pakistan LPG Association said.

Traders said the price of a 12kg cylinder jumped 56 per cent within days of the closure to 7,000 Pakistani rupees (US$25.30), or about 583 rupees per kg in the open market.

The government of Balochistan, the southern province that borders Iran, cited security and smuggling for the decision; Iran's foreign ministry said technical issues were to blame. Iran's ambassador later said Iran had imposed no restrictions, including on LPG exports, and blamed changes in Pakistan's import paperwork.

WALKING AWAY

Ali pays 600 rupees a day to rent his rickshaw, filling up with gas four or five times a day, at 300 to 400 rupees a time.

As well as daily expenses, Ali also pays 11,000 rupees a month for his home and has two young children to support.

Adding to his problems, passengers, he said, do not want to pay higher fares.

"For a trip that should cost 200 or 250 rupees, they might only offer 80, 100, or 150 rupees," Ali said.

Passenger Mohammad Ramzan said when a driver asked 500 rupees for a ride in the city, he offered half that. When the driver declined, he walked away, he said.

Inflation in Pakistan hit 9.6 per cent in October, and the central bank last week raised interest rates to 12 per cent, citing energy and wheat prices. Petrol hit a record 458 rupees a litre on Apr 3 and remains about 40 per cent above its pre-war price.

Back home at midday, Ali said his two boys still needed their lunch. He would go out again until late at night, he said, hoping to make enough to bring something for the children to eat at night.

articles.title: Indonesian police name suspects after 58 citizens lured to Russia to serve as mercenaries
articles.summary: The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.
articles.preview: The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones. JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities have uncovered a human trafficking syndicate involving 58 citizens who were allegedly recruited to work as mercenaries in Russia.
articles.body:
The Indonesian citizens were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but when arriving in Russia, were told to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.

JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities have uncovered a human trafficking syndicate involving 58 citizens who were allegedly recruited to work as mercenaries in Russia.

Thirteen people have been named as suspects, including two Russians and a Ukrainian citizen, the National Police Criminal Investigation Department (Bareskrim Polri) said on Monday (Nov 2).

Nurul Azizah, director of Bareskrim Polri's directorate of crimes against women and children and human trafficking, said at a press conference that the perpetrators used social media, job portals and messaging apps to lure victims with promises of lucrative overseas employment, state news agency Antara reported.

“We are coordinating through the Indonesian National Police’s International Relations Division and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Everything is still under further review,” Nurul said in response to CNA's queries on Tuesday.

The victims were initially offered jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after going through the recruitment process and being dispatched to Russia, they would be directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, undergo training and potentially be deployed to conflict zones.

“It is true that they did not directly offer jobs as mercenaries, but rather as logistics workers,” Nurul told reporters in Jakarta on Monday, as quoted by Kompas.

The victims were promised signing bonuses of up to US$35,000 and monthly salaries of around US$3,000.

Rita Wulandari Wibowo, director of Women and Child Protection at Metro Jaya Regional Police, said that recruiters also promised some victims child allowances of more than 3 million rupiah along with other benefits, Kompas reported.

“But in reality, none of these promises were fulfilled; the actual values were significantly lower, with some victims yet to receive any payments to this day,” Rita said on Monday.

The 58 individuals were identified after five police reports were made. Bareskrim Polri, together with the West Jakarta Metropolitan Police, Metro Jaya Regional Police and the Bogor Police, are investigating.

In a case investigated by the Bogor Police, victims were temporarily housed at a facility in Sukamantri Village in Bogor, with two suspects, identified by the initials FIK and STH, responsible for overseeing the victims’ living arrangements while they awaited departure.

Another suspect identified as MBH served as the financier throughout this process, covering recruitment expenses, lodging fees, medical check-ups, daily food costs and travelling arrangements, Kompas reported.

articles.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.
